RecordRoute: Auditing Agent Failures with Localization-Guided Diagnosis

Yifan Duan    Lihuan Li    Chao Xue    Siyuan Zheng    Du Yin    Flora D. Salim ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: UNSW Sydney, Australia Affiliation: yifan.duan3@unsw.edu.au, flora.salim@unsw.edu.au
Abstract

Auditing failed agent executions requires identifying the responsible actor, the earliest decisive step, and the error mode. Representative supervised methods either focus on step localization or predict multiple attribution targets from shared trajectory representations. These methods do not use the localization result to select the text for mode diagnosis. To address this limitation, we propose RecordRoute, which couples comparative localization with local diagnosis. Specifically, it represents each record with word and character features and learns to rank records through comparisons within each trajectory. The selected record supplies the actor and step, while its text and metadata drive mode prediction. On controlled-injection Who&When Pro, RecordRoute outperforms StepFinder and ASCon on all four official metrics. With actor and step predictions fixed, local diagnosis reaches 77.47% pooled joint accuracy versus 69.28% for full-trace diagnosis. On natural failures from TraceElephant and CatchBench POST, it outperforms these baselines and three open LLMs in localization.

1 Introduction

Language model agents increasingly execute long workflows using tools and coordinating with other agents (Yao et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024). When such a workflow fails, the final answer reveals the outcome but rarely identifies where the error began (Zhang et al., 2025b; Barke et al., 2026). A useful audit requires identifying the responsible actor, the earliest decisive step, and the error mode (Zhang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026). Locating a later symptom instead of its origin directs debugging toward the wrong component and obscures how the failure propagated (Fig. 1(a)).

Existing methods either ask a large language model to judge the trajectory or score candidate steps with a smaller model. LLM-based methods read, search, or verify the trajectory before generating a root-cause judgment (Zhu et al., 2026a; Xia et al., 2026). Some trace dependencies between steps (Wang et al., 2026b) or test hypotheses about the error (Li et al., 2026a) to separate its origin from later effects. MASPrism ranks steps using token likelihoods and attention weights from a small language model, without training (Liu et al., 2026b). StepFinder and ASCon learn step representations or joint agent and step representations from annotated failures (Zhu et al., 2026d; Jiang et al., 2026).

While promising, these approaches still struggle to separate a decisive error from its later symptoms (Yang et al., 2026). First, evidence of an earlier error can recur in later records (Pothuru, 2026). In Fig. 1(a), agent C repeats agent B’s incorrect claim, so the error appears at both steps. Tool names, exception fragments, and action wording can help distinguish such records. StepFinder and ASCon represent steps with dense embeddings. Dense representations can struggle with fine-grained lexical matching (Zhan et al., 2025). Second, these supervised models do not use the predicted step to select the text for mode diagnosis. StepFinder focuses on step localization, while ASCon predicts multiple attribution targets from shared trajectory representations. Yet actor and step identify a record, and mode describes the error in that record. A classifier that aggregates the full trace can instead mix the decisive error with its later consequences. These observations motivate comparing records within a trajectory while preserving their literal details, and diagnosing the error from the selected record.

To this end, we propose RecordRoute, a supervised method for locating and diagnosing agent failures. After removing identifying headers, it represents each record with word and character features. A pairwise ranker learns from feature differences between records in the same training trajectory. At inference, it scores records individually and selects the highest-scoring one. The selected record supplies the actor and step predictions. Its text, structural metadata, and actor identity provide the input for mode diagnosis (Fig. 1(b)).

On controlled-injection Who&When Pro, RecordRoute outperforms StepFinder and ASCon on all four official metrics. It reaches 90.86% pooled exact-step accuracy and 77.47% pooled joint accuracy. With actor and step predictions fixed, diagnosis from the selected record improves joint accuracy by 8.18 percentage points over full-trace diagnosis. The selected record contains a median of 19.77% of preprocessed trace tokens. On natural failures from TraceElephant and CatchBench POST, it ranks first in localization (Table 1).

This work makes three contributions.

  • •

    We develop a locator that combines word and character features with pairwise ranking within each trajectory, preserving record details while learning to identify the responsible actor and step.

  • •

    We condition mode diagnosis on the selected record’s text, structural metadata, and actor identity. The localization result determines the evidence used to diagnose the error.

  • •

    Ablations show that record representation, pairwise training, and local diagnosis each improve attribution on Who&When Pro. RecordRoute outperforms StepFinder and ASCon across all three benchmarks.

2 Related work

Failure-attribution benchmarks.

Failure taxonomies and attribution benchmarks cover coordination errors, responsible actors, decisive steps, and error types (Cemri et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2026a; Kong et al., 2026). Natural-failure and auditing benchmarks differ in what an attributor can observe and how predictions are scored (Chen et al., 2026; Barke et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026), while MP-Bench and LongRCA study ambiguous attributions and root causes in long trajectories (In et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). We train on the labels of each benchmark. The injected failures in Who&When Pro support component analysis, and the natural failures in TraceElephant and CatchBench test localization.

Trace reasoning and intervention.

Reasoning-based methods use multiple evaluators or scope narrowing (Zhu et al., 2026a; Xia et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026), dependency-guided search (Wang et al., 2026b; Rafi et al., 2026; Bakish et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026), constraint or hypothesis verification (Barke et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Qiao et al., 2026; Bi et al., 2026), and long-trace investigation (Zhu et al., 2026b; Qi et al., 2026). AgentRx also evaluates a variant that first predicts the critical step and then categorizes that step (Barke et al., 2026). Other work filters anomalous steps before attribution, uses attribution to guide reflection, or maps failures to editable system assets (Zhang et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026a; Yuan et al., 2026). RecordRoute instead learns a record ranker from annotated failures and diagnoses the error from the selected record without generating text.

Learned and efficient attribution.

StepFinder learns temporal step features. ASCon models reciprocal context between agents and steps with target-specific heads (Zhu et al., 2026d; Jiang et al., 2026). Other approaches exploit graphs, token likelihoods and attention weights from a small language model, or successful trajectories (Li et al., 2026b; Zhao, 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Yeh et al., 2026). AgenTracer post-trains a judge, HPFA contrasts failed and successful paths, and conformal attribution returns calibrated error regions (Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhu et al., 2026c; Feng et al., 2026). Unlike StepFinder and ASCon, RecordRoute represents records with word and character features and diagnoses the error from the selected record.

3 Problem formulation

Consider an LLM-based agent system with actor set 𝒜={a(1),…,a(Na)}\mathcal{A}=\{a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(N_{a})}\}. Its completed execution is recorded as an ordered trajectory T=(s1,…,snT)T=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n_{T}}), where each record has the form

si=(ci,ai,xi,zi),ai∈𝒜.s_{i}=(c_{i},a_{i},x_{i},z_{i}),\qquad a_{i}\in\mathcal{A}. (1)

Here cic_{i} is the benchmark’s step or round coordinate, aia_{i} identifies the executing actor, xix_{i} contains messages, reasoning text, or tool interactions, and ziz_{i} contains structural metadata such as record type and position. The sequence index ii orders the records, while cic_{i} preserves the benchmark coordinate. Several records can share cic_{i} when a round contains actions by multiple actors. We denote the observed coordinate set by 𝒞T={ci}i=1nT\mathcal{C}_{T}=\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{T}} and the available task query by qq.

Given a failed trajectory, attribution identifies the responsible actor, the earliest decisive step, and its error mode. Let ℳ={m1,…,mNm}\mathcal{M}=\{m_{1},\ldots,m_{N_{m}}\} denote the benchmark’s error-mode taxonomy. The annotation is represented by 𝒢T=(A∗,C∗,m∗)\mathcal{G}_{T}=(A^{*},C^{*},m^{*}), where A∗⊆𝒜A^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{A} contains accepted responsible actors, C∗⊆𝒞TC^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{T} contains accepted coordinates for the decisive error, and m∗∈ℳm^{*}\in\mathcal{M} is its mode label.

The objective is to learn an attribution function

fθ​(T,q)\displaystyle f_{\theta}(T,q) =(a^,c^,m^),\displaystyle=(\hat{a},\hat{c},\hat{m}), (2)
(a^,c^,m^)\displaystyle(\hat{a},\hat{c},\hat{m}) ∈𝒜×𝒞T×ℳ.\displaystyle\in\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{C}_{T}\times\mathcal{M}.

The predicted actor and coordinate specify where the error is attributed, and the predicted mode describes its type. A correct attribution satisfies a^∈A∗\hat{a}\in A^{*}, c^∈C∗\hat{c}\in C^{*}, and m^=m∗\hat{m}=m^{*}, where actor matches follow the official rules of each benchmark. On TraceElephant and CatchBench, we evaluate step localization.

4 Methodology

RecordRoute extracts features for each record, ranks the candidates, and derives the attribution from the selected record. Unlike ASCon, which predicts modes from an agent representation and pooled representations of its steps (Jiang et al., 2026), our mode classifier reads the text of the record selected by the locator. We represent records with word and character features and train a locator LwL_{w} through comparisons within each trajectory. The selected record supplies the actor and step, and a classifier HUH_{U} predicts its mode, which decomposes Equation 2 as

i^\displaystyle\hat{i} =Lw​(T,q),\displaystyle=L_{w}(T,q), (3)
fθ​(T,q)\displaystyle f_{\theta}(T,q) =(ai^,ci^,HU​(si^,q)).\displaystyle=(a_{\hat{i}},c_{\hat{i}},H_{U}(s_{\hat{i}},q)).

4.1 Record feature extraction

Tool names, exception fragments, and action wording can help distinguish a decisive error from records that repeat its symptoms. We retain these cues with word and character TF-IDF features. Word features represent individual terms and short action phrases. Character features retain substrings within tool identifiers and error messages, so records can share features even when their complete tokens differ. Together, the two views expose action wording and local string details to the locator.

Before encoding a record, we remove headers that identify its actor and coordinate. This prevents the rendered headers from contributing lexical features to localization. The original actor and coordinate remain attached to the candidate for output after localization. Each record remains a separate candidate, preserving the correspondence between its text, actor, and coordinate throughout encoding.

For record body xix_{i} and task query qq, we concatenate four feature blocks (Fig. 2(a))

ϕ(xi,q)=[\displaystyle\phi(x_{i},q)=[ vw​(xi),vc​(xi),\displaystyle v_{w}(x_{i}),v_{c}(x_{i}), (4)
vw​(xi)⊙vw​(q),\displaystyle v_{w}(x_{i})\odot v_{w}(q),
⟨vw(xi),vw(q)⟩].\displaystyle\langle v_{w}(x_{i}),v_{w}(q)\rangle].

vwv_{w} uses word unigrams and bigrams, and vcv_{c} uses character n-grams of lengths three to five within word boundaries. Elementwise multiplication ⊙\odot retains which terms are shared with the query, allowing the ranker to assign different weights to individual matches. The inner product gives an overall measure of lexical overlap. These two blocks connect record wording to the task description while retaining the record’s own word and character features. When queries are unavailable or omitted, we set qq to the empty string and both overlap blocks become zero. The resulting representation ϕi=ϕ⁡(xi,q)\phi_{i}=\phi(x_{i},q) is the input to the locator.

4.2 Pairwise record ranking

Localization requires distinguishing the decisive error from other records in the same trajectory. We train the locator to rank records accepted by the annotation above the remaining candidates, then score each record individually at inference (Fig. 2(b)). We use a coordinate target or a joint actor and coordinate target, indexed by r∈{coord,joint}r\in\{\mathrm{coord},\mathrm{joint}\}, to define candidate labels

yi(r)={𝟏[ci∈C∗],r=coord,𝟏[ai∈A∗∧ci∈C∗],r=joint.y_{i}^{(r)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{1}[c_{i}\in C^{*}],&r=\mathrm{coord},\\ \mathbf{1}[a_{i}\in A^{*}\wedge c_{i}\in C^{*}],&r=\mathrm{joint}.\end{cases} (5)

Actor membership follows the official matching rules in Section 3. Coordinate targets apply to fine-grained records, while joint targets distinguish actors within a shared round. The public trace schema determines the target before model fitting. For each target, we fit a separate locator and mode classifier on the same training split, and write ww and UU for the parameters of the applicable variant.

For example, suppose actors A and B both act in round cc, and A’s record is annotated as the decisive error. A coordinate target accepts both records at cc. A joint target accepts A’s record and makes B’s record a comparison candidate. This allows the training labels to distinguish two actors even when their records share the same step coordinate.

StepFinder uses a cross-entropy loss over candidate steps for localization (Zhu et al., 2026d). We instead train on feature differences between pairs of records with different labels. For a fixed target, write yi=yi(r)y_{i}=y_{i}^{(r)} and let 𝒫T={(i,j)∣1≤i,j≤nT,yi≠yj}\mathcal{P}_{T}=\{(i,j)\mid 1\leq i,j\leq n_{T},\ y_{i}\neq y_{j}\} contain all ordered pairs with different labels in each training trajectory. Each informative pair appears in both orientations, with feature differences and signed preference labels

di​j\displaystyle d_{ij} =ϕi−ϕj,\displaystyle=\phi_{i}-\phi_{j}, (6)
ℓi​j\displaystyle\ell_{ij} =2𝟏[yi>yj]−1.\displaystyle=2\mathbf{1}[y_{i}>y_{j}]-1.

These pairs compare the annotated error with other observations of the same failed execution, including later symptoms. When several records are accepted, each is compared with the remaining candidates, without imposing an ordering among accepted records. For a linear score ρi=w⊤​ϕi\rho_{i}=w^{\top}\phi_{i}, the score difference satisfies

w⊤​di​j=ρi−ρj.w^{\top}d_{ij}=\rho_{i}-\rho_{j}. (7)

Thus, training on feature differences directly learns the score ordering used for selection. Features with equal values in both records cancel, so the comparison depends on the differences between the two candidates.

Over the training trajectories 𝒟tr+\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{+} with nonempty 𝒫T\mathcal{P}_{T}, we minimize the regularized pairwise logistic loss (Burges et al., 2005)

ℒrank​(w)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rank}}(w) =λ2​‖w‖22\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{2}\|w\|_{2}^{2} (8)
+∑T∈𝒟tr+1|𝒫T|∑(i,j)∈𝒫T\displaystyle+\sum_{T\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{+}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{T}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_{T}}
log⁡(1+exp⁡(−ℓi​j​w⊤​di​j)).\displaystyle\log\big(1+\exp(-\ell_{ij}w^{\top}d_{ij})\big).

Here λ\lambda controls regularization. The loss encourages accepted records to receive higher scores than other candidates in the same trajectory. The factor 1/|𝒫T|1/|\mathcal{P}_{T}| normalizes pair weights within each informative trajectory to sum to one, which keeps trajectories with more candidates from dominating the training loss. We fit this objective with linear logistic regression. A shared intercept cancels when subtracting two record scores, so the ranker is fitted without an intercept.

At inference, the locator scores each record once and selects the record with the highest score

ρi\displaystyle\rho_{i} =w⊤​ϕi,\displaystyle=w^{\top}\phi_{i}, (9)
i^\displaystyle\hat{i} =arg⁡max1≤i≤nT⁡ρi.\displaystyle=\arg\max_{1\leq i\leq n_{T}}\rho_{i}.

We resolve score ties in favor of the earlier record. The selected index i^\hat{i} identifies the record passed to the attribution stage. Pair construction is used only during training. At inference, the number of score evaluations grows linearly with the number of records, followed by one mode prediction.

4.3 Attribution from the selected record

Attribution begins by reading the actor and coordinate from the selected record’s retained header, giving (a^,c^)=(ai^,ci^)(\hat{a},\hat{c})=(a_{\hat{i}},c_{\hat{i}}) (Fig. 2(c)). These predictions refer to the same execution record even when several actors share a round coordinate.

The remaining question is which error mode describes the selected action. A failed trajectory may contain the initiating error, reactions to that error, and actions that are themselves valid. Combining their text gives the classifier evidence about several events, although the requested mode describes the error in the selected record. We therefore use the selected record as the textual input to diagnosis. This connects the predicted mode to the same execution record that supplies the actor and coordinate.

The record’s actor identity and structural metadata provide context for interpreting its action. We encode the record text with the available task query and concatenate the resulting features with its actor identity and structural metadata

hi=[ϕ~​(xi,q),η⁡(ai,zi)].h_{i}=[\widetilde{\phi}(x_{i},q),\eta(a_{i},z_{i})]. (10)

ϕ~\widetilde{\phi} uses the TF-IDF construction in Equation 4 and is fitted separately on records at accepted coordinates, indexed by ℐTmode={i∣ci∈C∗}\mathcal{I}_{T}^{\mathrm{mode}}=\{i\mid c_{i}\in C^{*}\}. The metadata map η\eta combines standardized numeric features, including record length, trajectory length, and relative position, with indicators for record type and actor identity and their interactions with framework and task domain. Local diagnosis thus restricts the execution text to the selected record while retaining task and structural context.

A class-balanced linear SVM assigns a margin to each error mode. With classifier parameters U={(um,bm)}m∈ℳU=\{(u_{m},b_{m})\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}}, the prediction is

m^\displaystyle\hat{m} =HU​(si^,q)\displaystyle=H_{U}(s_{\hat{i}},q) (11)
=arg⁡maxm∈ℳ⁡(um⊤​hi^+bm).\displaystyle=\arg\max_{m\in\mathcal{M}}(u_{m}^{\top}h_{\hat{i}}+b_{m}).

During training, we fit UU to examples (hi,m∗)(h_{i},m^{*}) for i∈ℐTmodei\in\mathcal{I}_{T}^{\mathrm{mode}}, with per-record weights 1/|ℐTmode|1/|\mathcal{I}_{T}^{\mathrm{mode}}|. Normalizing these weights prevents trajectories with more records at accepted coordinates from receiving extra sample weight. Restricting the training examples to these records associates each mode label with its annotated coordinates. The locator and diagnostic classifier are fitted separately using the same training split. At test time, the classifier diagnoses the record selected by the locator, so localization errors remain visible in joint attribution.

All feature maps and models are fitted using training data alone. For step localization, we fit and apply the locator alone. Preprocessing and model settings appear in Appendix A.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Benchmarks.

Our primary evaluation uses all 6,257 failures with text traces released by Who&When Pro (Liu et al., 2026a). They contain 38,140 candidate records from eight agent frameworks and 16 task benchmarks. TraceElephant (Chen et al., 2026) contains 218 natural failures and 5,898 candidate steps from three agent systems. CatchBench (Zhao et al., 2026) defines PRE, LIVE, and POST audit settings. Our method performs retrospective localization, which corresponds to POST. We use its Who&When subset, containing 126 natural failures and 1,099 candidate steps.

Baselines.

We compare with StepFinder (Zhu et al., 2026d) and ASCon (Jiang et al., 2026) on all three benchmarks. We use their official architectures and training budgets. Both use our mode classifier on Who&When Pro. ASCon retains its independent actor and step heads. We also evaluate GRADE exec-rank, auditable blast share, and PyGOD DOMINANT on all three benchmarks, adapting the CatchBench POST implementations (Zhao et al., 2026). These step rankers use the same mode classifier on Who&When Pro. On CatchBench, we report the published POST results for auditable and DOMINANT. Simple baselines include random selection, BM25, selection of the first, middle, or last step, and a learned relative-position baseline on all three benchmarks. We evaluate Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025), Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1 (Jiang et al., 2024), and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) without benchmark-specific training on the complete evaluation sets of all three benchmarks. Their prompts and input settings appear in Appendix B.1.

Evaluation Metrics.

On Who&When Pro, we report pooled exact accuracy for each target and for the complete tuple using the annotation-matching criteria in Section 3. Joint accuracy requires all three targets to be correct. We also report the official aggregates. Who is actor accuracy macro-averaged over multi-agent frameworks, When is exact-step accuracy macro-averaged over frameworks, What is global macro-F1 over the 14 observed error-mode classes, and All is joint accuracy macro-averaged over frameworks. TraceElephant uses exact-step accuracy. CatchBench uses Top-1 and Top-3 accuracy and mean reciprocal rank (MRR).

Implementation Details.

We use five-fold cross-validation, grouping Who&When Pro and TraceElephant by task query and following CatchBench’s official grouped splits. Supervised methods use the same folds within each benchmark. On TraceElephant, we select CC by cross-validation within each training fold. For supervised methods, Who&When Pro and TraceElephant record bodies are limited to 800 characters, while CatchBench retains the original step length. On Who&When Pro, StepFinder and ASCon use three training seeds. Our CatchBench results average five split seeds. Preprocessing, training settings, and aggregation details appear in Appendix A.

5.2 Main Results

Table 1 compares methods across three benchmarks. RecordRoute learns from labeled failures, while the three open LLMs receive no benchmark training labels.

Who&When Pro.

RecordRoute achieves the highest scores on all four attribution metrics. It reaches 88.50 When and 63.67 All, compared with 73.28 and 48.53 for StepFinder, and 77.06 and 52.30 for ASCon. The All gains of 15.14 and 11.37 percentage points measure improvements in joint actor, step, and mode prediction. RecordRoute also improves Who and What over ASCon by 14.86 and 9.99 points. Both neural baselines share our mode classifier, keeping the diagnosis model fixed while the selected records differ. The supervised text-based methods also exceed the structural rankers in When and All. GRADE exec-rank, the strongest structural baseline, reaches 45.96 When and 32.88 All. Qwen2.5-14B leads the three open LLMs with 62.34 When and 15.91 All. Qwen scores 14.05 on What, compared with 70.05 for RecordRoute, indicating that the gap includes diagnosis of the error mode. RecordRoute’s gains over this zero-shot baseline cover both localization and complete attribution.

TraceElephant.

The localization advantage also appears on naturally occurring failures. We train and evaluate each supervised method on TraceElephant using identical folds grouped by task. RecordRoute reaches 27.06% exact-step accuracy, compared with 18.81% for ASCon and 11.01% for StepFinder. The gains are 8.26 and 16.06 percentage points, respectively. Qwen2.5-14B, the strongest evaluated open LLM on this benchmark, reaches 23.85% with the official prompt. BM25 reaches 7.80%, while GRADE exec-rank reaches 8.72%. Both neural baselines improve on retrieval and execution features, and RecordRoute improves on both neural baselines. This ordering among the supervised methods is consistent with Who&When Pro despite the different agent systems and source of failures. Task grouping across systems excludes each test query from the corresponding training folds.

CatchBench.

RecordRoute achieves the highest mean Top-1, Top-3, and MRR scores among all methods in Table 1 on CatchBench POST. It reaches 37.46% Top-1, 77.78% Top-3, and 0.590 MRR. ASCon is the closest supervised competitor, with 34.92% Top-1, 72.54% Top-3, and 0.567 MRR. The open LLMs also score lower when asked to rank all candidates. Mixtral leads them in Top-1 and MRR at 19.84% and 0.424, while Qwen reaches 53.17% Top-3. The comparison with BM25 illustrates why both first-choice accuracy and candidate coverage matter. BM25 reaches 65.87% Top-3 but only 12.70% Top-1, often including the fault without placing it first. RecordRoute improves both measures and the overall ranking measured by MRR. Its top three candidates contain the annotated fault in over three quarters of cases, providing a short list for subsequent inspection. Pooled scores and results across training seeds appear in Appendix C.

5.3 Generalization

We evaluate whether RecordRoute can localize errors in task benchmarks and agent frameworks excluded from training. For each task benchmark, we train the locator on the other 15 benchmarks after removing matching task queries. The locator receives only record text and achieves 81.99% pooled and 78.77% macro exact-step accuracy (Figure 3(a)), outperforming BM25 and the last-step baseline on all 16 benchmarks. These results show that the locator can identify errors on new task benchmarks using the execution records alone, without access to the task query.

We further test whether this localization capability extends to unseen agent frameworks by excluding each framework and its matching task queries from training. RecordRoute outperforms StepFinder on seven of the eight frameworks and reaches 54.97% macro exact-step accuracy, compared with 44.41% for StepFinder (Figure 3(b)). The gains across these frameworks show that the learned ranking remains useful when the agent framework changes. Pooled accuracy is 49.03%, compared with 49.38% for the last-step baseline.

5.4 Ablation Study

5.4.1 Record representation and ranking

We compare sparse record features with Qwen3 embeddings at 128 and 1024 dimensions under pointwise and pairwise learning. All six configurations use the same folds, step targets, and mode classifier, with blank task queries and C=1C=1.

Table 2(a) identifies two sources of localization accuracy. At the stronger 1024-dimensional dense control, the word and character representation contributes 17.41 exact-step points. Pairwise learning contributes another 3.36 points, with an interaction of +0.62+0.62 points. At StepFinder’s 128-dimensional setting, the corresponding effects are 25.35 and 3.71 points. The sparse pairwise model exceeds the 1024-dimensional dense control by 17.72 points. Its 90.41% rises to the final 90.86% with query overlap and targets that distinguish actors within shared steps.

Word and character features lead under both objectives, while pairwise learning improves each representation. The same ordering holds for joint accuracy, reaching 77.13% with sparse pairwise training versus 62.92% with 1024-dimensional embeddings under the same mode classifier.

On CatchBench, pairwise learning improves all three ranking metrics with the same record features (Table 2(b)), supporting comparative ranking on natural failures. Top-1 accuracy rises from 34.44% to 37.46%.

With task queries removed and content words masked, the locator still achieves 86.75% exact-step accuracy on Who&When Pro (Table 8(a)).

5.4.2 Diagnostic evidence

With actor and step predictions fixed, we compare the selected record and the concatenated full trace using the same classifier design, metadata, folds, and regularization (Table 3). Diagnosis from the selected record reaches 77.47% joint accuracy, compared with 69.28% from the full trace, a gain of 8.18 points. This comparison supports using the locator’s selection to choose evidence for the mode classifier.

Mean and max pooling reach 43.92% and 52.63% joint accuracy. These controls combine class margins from individual records, whereas concatenation combines their text. Local diagnosis exceeds both forms of aggregation, using only the record selected by the locator.

Learned aggregation of predictions from individual records reaches 64.95% joint accuracy, leaving a 12.51-point gap. The selected record therefore remains more effective when the full-trace control processes records individually before combining their predictions. With the same step predictions, independent actor and full-trace mode classifiers reach 65.41%. Removing text from the selected record while retaining its structure and actor reduces joint accuracy to 44.38%, showing that its text contributes information beyond the metadata.

After both diagnostic models are retrained with content words masked, the selected record remains better than learned full-trace aggregation, with 72.81% versus 57.41% joint accuracy (Table 8(b)).

On the 597 trajectories in which multiple actors share step coordinates, defining positive records by both actor and step reduces their mean number from 3.23 to 1.35. Twelve previously incorrect joint predictions become correct and one becomes incorrect, with predictions for unique coordinates unchanged.

With raw-text input, median inference takes 9.32 ms on CPU for RecordRoute and 66.61 ms on GPU for StepFinder. Efficiency measurements and diagnostic controls using LLMs appear in Appendices A and B.2, respectively.

6 Conclusion

We presented RecordRoute, a supervised method for identifying the responsible actor, earliest decisive step, and error mode. It combines word and character features with pairwise ranking within each trajectory. The selected record supplies the actor and step, while its text and metadata guide mode prediction. Experiments show gains over StepFinder and ASCon across three benchmarks, with ablations supporting all three components. These findings support using localization to select the evidence for diagnosis.

Appendix A Implementation Details

Data and preprocessing.

We group Who&When Pro and TraceElephant into five folds by the task query normalized to lowercase with whitespace collapsed. Vocabularies, scalers, and classifiers are fitted on the training folds. Record headers are removed from the locator input. Record bodies are limited to 800 characters, retaining 58% from the beginning and 42% from the end. TraceElephant inputs include outputs and linked tool results. CatchBench uses its official grouped folds and five split seeds, retaining each record’s original length. Both natural-failure benchmarks use record text without task queries. For the generalization experiments, training excludes the evaluated task benchmark or framework and all matching task queries.

Features and classifiers.

Word TF-IDF uses unigrams and bigrams with at most 30,000 features. Character TF-IDF uses n-grams of lengths three to five within word boundaries with at most 20,000 features. Both use sublinear term frequency and a minimum document frequency of two. The pairwise logistic ranker has no intercept and uses C=1C=1 on Who&When Pro and CatchBench. The class-balanced linear SVM for mode prediction also uses C=1C=1. On TraceElephant, five-fold validation within each training fold selects CC from {0.01,0.03,0.1,0.3,1,3,10}\{0.01,0.03,0.1,0.3,1,3,10\} by pooled exact-step accuracy, with ties favoring the smaller value. The five selected values are 1,3,3,1,0.31,3,3,1,0.3.

Baselines and seeds.

StepFinder and ASCon use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025c) with 128-dimensional record embeddings and 32-dimensional actor embeddings. StepFinder trains for up to 50 epochs with batch size 16 and patience 10. ASCon uses its public Task-1 architecture and 12-epoch schedule. Both use the same inner development split and training seeds 42, 43, and 44 on Who&When Pro, with the mode classifier refitted in each fold. ASCon retains its independent actor head. Natural-failure runs use training seed 42+fold42+\text{fold}. CatchBench reserves 10% of each training fold for checkpoint selection, and its results average the five official split seeds. Framework evaluation uses seed 42 for StepFinder.

Random selection uses a fixed trace-ID hash. BM25 ranks records against the task query. First and Last rank records chronologically and in reverse, and Middle ranks by distance from the lower midpoint. Position uses class-balanced logistic regression on relative position. GRADE retains its eight public execution features and uses C=1C=1. The graph baselines assume full-context dependencies, under which auditable ranks records chronologically. DOMINANT fits unlabeled run graphs with two layers, hidden width 32, 40 epochs, and seed 0 on CPU. Its feature scaling and graph fitting use the unlabeled dataset, while its mode classifier uses only the corresponding training folds.

Diagnostic controls.

The concatenation control reads the full trace. Mean and max pooling combine class margins from individual records. Learned aggregation fits a classifier on their means, maxima, and standard deviations using inner out-of-fold predictions. The separate-actor control fits an actor ranker on aggregated actor text and a mode classifier on the full trace. These controls retain the same step predictions, feature family, folds, and regularization as local diagnosis.

Efficiency.

Table 4 reports measurements on 256 trajectories using one RTX A5000 host. Timings include feature construction, localization, and diagnosis, excluding model loading and disk I/O. After one warm-up, we use ten cached-path repeats and three raw StepFinder repeats. Training takes 159.75 seconds per fold for RecordRoute and 474.52 for StepFinder.

Appendix B LLM Experiments

B.1 Open LLM baselines

Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct receive no benchmark training examples. On Who&When Pro, the prompt supplies the official trace rendering, task query, and error taxonomy, and requests the actor, step coordinate, and error mode. Explicit coordinates and taxonomy names are normalized before official scoring. Missing or unrecognized fields count as incorrect.

For Who&When Pro and CatchBench, inference uses vLLM 0.26.0, BF16 weights, greedy decoding, seed 0, a 30,000-token input limit, and up to 512 output tokens. Longer inputs retain every record header and each body’s beginning and end under a common character cap. All cases remain in the evaluation. CatchBench prompts request a ranking of all candidate step IDs. Incomplete rankings receive a format retry, followed if needed by decoding constrained to complete permutations of the candidate IDs. The same ranking determines Top-1, Top-3, and MRR.

On TraceElephant, Qwen uses the official all-at-once prompt, while Mixtral and Llama use the shared direct-attribution prompt. Inference uses BF16 weights, greedy decoding, and a 512-token output limit. All 218 cases are scored, including the 57 Mixtral answers without a valid global step coordinate, which count as incorrect.

B.2 Diagnosis with selected records

We evaluate Claude Sonnet 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the same 128 Who&When Pro cases, with 16 from each framework. The sample and prompts are fixed before inference. Both models receive the task query and public error taxonomy. Direct attribution requests all three targets from the full trace. The RecordRoute conditions fix its predicted actor and step and request the mode from either the selected record or the full trace. BM25 uses the same local diagnosis prompt with its own selected record. RecordRoute uses labeled training failures from the target frameworks, while the LLMs receive no training examples.

We use claude-sonnet-5-5 with high effort and deepseek-flash with reasoning disabled. Each condition uses matching instructions and output fields across providers. The output limit is 4,096 tokens, with one retry at 8,192 tokens for truncated answers. The calls were made in October 2026, and every condition is scored on all 128 cases.

Table 5 shows that RecordRoute with local diagnosis raises joint accuracy from 19.53% to 41.41% for Sonnet and from 20.31% to 36.72% for DeepSeek. Both models also obtain higher mode accuracy from the selected record than from the full trace at the same predicted location. Local diagnosis reduces API input tokens by 54.86% and 57.00%, respectively, relative to direct attribution. These token counts exclude locator training and inference. Supplying predicted locations and selected records improves both LLMs on this cohort. The original RecordRoute classifier reaches 58.59% joint accuracy on the same cases.

Appendix C Supplementary Results

Pooled results and training seeds.

Tables 7 and 7 report pooled exact accuracy and individual training seeds on Who&When Pro. Folds and checkpoint rules are fixed across seeds.

Record content.

Table 8 reports localization and diagnosis after changes to record text. Code canonicalization standardizes Markdown fences and <code> tags. Content masking replaces content words and numbers while retaining punctuation, word lengths, and a fixed vocabulary of function and heading words. Masked localization removes task queries. Both diagnostic models are retrained on masked records with actor and step predictions fixed.

Individual benchmarks and frameworks.

Tables 10 and 10 give the individual results underlying Figure 3.
